extracted.intended_audience: improv students and performers training in long-form Harold (particularly iO Chicago students/faculty)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and an evaluation checklist for performing and teaching the Harold long-form improv at iO Chicago, emphasizing universe-establishment, group mind, patience, and rewarding audience pattern-recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Harold (structure and function)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Harold is a 25–30 minute form with three rounds of three scenes, intercut with group games and a final tying-together. Its function is structural: TRAIN the team to find connections between disparate scenes that weren't planned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performances should follow the three-round/three-scenes architecture with group games and a final tying-together; the form's purpose is to produce emergent connections across scenes rather than isolated jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group Mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Group Mind is the felt sense that the team is improvising as ONE intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: simultaneous edits, identical thoughts in tag-outs, callbacks no one set up. Build group mind by playing together for years, not by trying to manufacture it in performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patience
rubrics_metrics.description: The first scene of a Harold sets the universe. Don't try to be funny in the first 60 seconds; ESTABLISH. The funny will arrive when the structure has earned it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beginners often panic and force jokes; experienced performers wait for the structure to develop. Prioritize establishing relationships, locations, and stakes early rather than immediate punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection (third-round reward)
rubrics_metrics.description: The third round of the Harold rewards CONNECTIONS made by the team. The audience laughs at recognizing connections the team also just discovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for pattern emergence and callbacks that feel discovered rather than forced; the emotional/aesthetic 'magic' of long-form is when the audience's recognition mirrors the team's discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Del Close maxim: 'Treat the audience as poets.'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Treat the audience as poets." (Quoted Del Close maxim used by faculty.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame material in ways that invites the audience to find meaning and pattern rather than spelling out obvious jokes; respect audience intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Del Close maxim: 'Trust your fellow players.'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Trust your fellow players." (Quoted Del Close maxim used by faculty.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make choices that support and accept teammates' offers; prioritizing ensemble support over one-player spotlight builds stronger scenes and connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Del Close maxim: 'Don't try to be funny; the funny will come.'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Don't try to be funny; the funny will come." (Quoted Del Close maxim used by faculty.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on truthful, clear choices and the game's discovery; avoid forcing jokes early—humor should emerge from established premises and patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Del Close maxim: 'Find the GAME of the scene.'
rubrics_metrics.description: "Find the GAME of the scene." (Originated here, refined at UCB.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the recurring comic pattern or escalation in a scene (the 'game') and play it clearly; use the game's clarity to drive callbacks and inter-scene connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: iO Working Rubric — 1: Establish the universe in first scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the first scene establish the universe before trying for laughs?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether relationships, location, tone, and stakes were set early so later beats and callbacks have grounding; penalize premature joke-chasing that undermines setup.

rubrics_metrics.name: iO Working Rubric — 2: Organic inter-scene connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Did connections across scenes emerge organically?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for links that feel discovered by the team in performance rather than contrived; connections should arise from honest scene choices and callbacks, not telegraphed stitching.

rubrics_metrics.name: iO Working Rubric — 3: Team displayed group mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the team display group mind?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess for indicators like simultaneous edits, matching tag-outs, and unplanned callbacks showing ensemble cohesion; note whether the team appeared to be improvising as a single intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: iO Working Rubric — 4: Third round rewarded audience pattern recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the third round REWARD the audience's pattern recognition?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the final tying-together produced satisfying recognition for the audience—moments where previously disparate elements connect and produce laughter or insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: iO Working Rubric — 5: Trust in fellow players
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you trust your fellow players?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure performers' risk-taking and supportiveness: did individuals accept offers and build on them rather than blocking or undermining teammates?

rubrics_metrics.name: iO Working Rubric — 6: Treat the audience as poets
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you treat the audience as poets?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the performance respected audience intelligence and allowed them to discover patterns and meaning, rather than spoon-feeding punchlines or obvious explanations.
